# Logarithms (`logarithms`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: helped by decimal_fractions
- Core idea: Write every positive number as a power of ten; the exponent is its logarithm. Since powers multiply by adding exponents, log(a x b) = log a + log b, a table of logarithms turns multiplication into addition, division into subtraction and roots into division by 2 or 3. A table can be started from coincidences: 2 to the 10th is 1024, close to 10 cubed, so log 2 is about 0.3 (0.30103 to five decimal places); also log 3 = 0.47712 and log 7 = 0.84510, and all other values follow from products and careful interpolation. For astronomers and navigators this cuts hours of multiplication to minutes.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the logarithm of a sum is the sum of the logarithms.
  - Calling Napier's original logarithms natural logarithms. His 1614 table has a different definition; base 10 came from Briggs in 1617–1624 and base e later.
  - Underestimating the labour. A usable table needs thousands of values to 5–7 places and must be printed without errors.
  - Reading between table entries without interpolation.
- History: islamic: c. 1000 – Ibn Yunus (Cairo) uses a product-to-sum rule for cosines, the basis of later prosthaphaeresis; europe: 1544 – Stifel compares arithmetic and geometric sequences; 1580s prosthaphaeresis (trigonometric product formulas) at Tycho's observatory; 1614 John Napier, Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio; 1620 Jost Buergi independently; 1624 Henry Briggs, Arithmetica logarithmica (base 10); china: 1653 – logarithm tables introduced by the Jesuit Smogulecki and Xue Fengzuo
- Read:
  - John Napier, Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio (1614)
  - Eli Maor, e: The Story of a Number (1994)
